investment_summary:
Rocket Lab delivered strong top-line momentum in 2025. Revenue rose 38% to $601.8 million, gross margin expanded to 34.4% from 26.6%, and the operating margin improved to -38.1% from -43.6% [1]. Launch cadence rose to 21 missions from 16, and total backlog reached $1,847.3 million, of which $1,371.7 million related to Space Systems [1]. The business is scaling and becoming more efficient, a trend supported by the peer comparison on gross margin and EBITDA margin [4].

The financial trajectory is less comfortable. The net loss widened to $198.2 million, operating cash flow was -$165.5 million, and free cash flow reached about -$321.8 million [1]. Liquidity is strong, with cash of $828.7 million and a current ratio of about 4.1x [1]. Funding, however, depends on equity markets: at-the-market issuance raised $1,119.5 million in 2025, and management expects losses to continue for at least the next 12 months [1].

Valuation is the central debate. The stock closed at $70.20, with a market capitalization of about $42.8 billion and a 52-week range of $14.71 to $99.58 [2]. Analyst consensus carries a Buy rating with a mean target of $93.15 and a range of $58 to $127 [3]. That target is dated after the filing and should be read as a later view. The trailing EV/Sales multiple of about 67x is far above every peer in the group [4]. Key risks include reliance on government customers, which represent about 47% of revenue [1], and the Neutron first launch, now targeted for Q4 2026 after a January 2026 tank qualification failure [1]. The investment case hinges on converting backlog into profitable, on-schedule deliveries while managing continued dilution.
business_overview:
Rocket Lab Corporation describes itself as an end-to-end space company that provides launch services, spacecraft design and manufacturing, spacecraft components, optical systems, and on-orbit constellation management, with the stated aim of making access to space faster, easier, and more affordable [1]. The commercial space economy is being driven by miniaturization and by demand for communications, Earth observation, meteorology, and navigation satellites, and the company serves that demand across the full mission lifecycle. Its Electron small launch vehicle has completed 75 successful missions and delivered more than 200 spacecraft through December 31, 2025, and the company states that Electron was the second most frequently launched orbital rocket in 2025 [1]. The business reports two revenue lines: Space Systems, which generated $402.8 million in 2025, and Launch Services, which generated $199.0 million [1].

The technology base rests on carbon composite tanks and structures, electric turbo-pump 3D-printed Rutherford engines (over 800 flown), and a kick stage that can be converted into an operational spacecraft [1]. Design and manufacturing are vertically integrated across the United States, New Zealand, and Canada. Launch infrastructure includes LC-1 in New Zealand, which supports up to 120 launches per year; LC-2 in Virginia, licensed for 8 missions per year; and LC-3, under construction to support Neutron, a reusable medium-lift vehicle targeting about 13,000 kg to low Earth orbit [1]. During 2025 the company acquired GEOST for $132.4 million in cash and signed the Space Development Agency Tranche 3 agreement, worth up to $816 million [1]. Its product set spans Electron (up to 300 kg to low Earth orbit), the HASTE suborbital vehicle, the Photon spacecraft, and components such as reaction wheels, star trackers, solar cells, and optical systems [1].

From a market perspective, Rocket Lab shares closed at $70.20 with a market capitalization of about $42.8 billion, against a 52-week range of $14.71 to $99.58 [2]. Analyst consensus carries a Buy rating with a mean target of $93.15, within a range of $58 to $127 [3]. A market value of this size against $601.8 million of revenue means investors are paying for growth that has not yet reached profitability, a theme that runs through the rest of this report [1][2].
market_position:
Rocket Lab's end markets are both governmental and commercial, and its operations are split geographically. Launches take place from New Zealand and Virginia, and manufacturing is located in California, New Zealand, New Mexico, and Arizona, serving customers in the United States and abroad [1]. Government customers include the U.S. Department of War, NASA, DARPA, and the National Reconnaissance Office, while commercial customers include BlackSky, Canon, Kinéis, Capella Space, Planet, OHB Group, and Synspective [1]. Government demand is a growing share of the business: U.S. government and U.S. prime contractor revenue, including subcontracts, reached about 47% of 2025 revenue, up from 33% in 2024 and 31% in 2023 [1]. That shift means the company's growth is increasingly tied to federal budgets and procurement decisions rather than to commercial demand alone.

Customer concentration is high. The top five customers accounted for about 49% of 2025 revenue, and the top five backlog customers held about 77% of year-end backlog [1]. Backlog totaled $1,847.3 million, of which $1,371.7 million related to Space Systems, including the SDA Tranche 3 award and the GEOST acquisition [1]. The company also notes that the October 1, 2025 government shutdown delayed contract awards and payments, and that reduced workforce levels at critical sites such as Wallops affected operations [1]. Large backlog supports revenue visibility, but the revenue base depends on a small group of buyers and on federal budget timing. Headcount rose from about 1,400 employees in December 2022 to more than 2,600 by December 31, 2025, which reflects the scale of the build-out behind that backlog [1].

Market share is not disclosed in the filing. The company describes itself as a leader in small launch and states that Electron was the second most frequently launched orbital rocket in 2025 [1]. It competes with SpaceX, Northrop Grumman, Firefly, and others, several of which are larger and better resourced, and some foreign competitors receive government support [1]. Against this field, Rocket Lab's position rests on flight heritage, vertical integration, and a rising launch cadence. Its ability to hold share while Neutron is developed will depend on converting backlog into delivered missions on schedule [1].
operating_results:
Revenue increased 38% to $601.8 million in 2025 from $436.2 million, with both lines growing [1]. Space Systems rose $91.9 million (30%) to $402.8 million, driven by spacecraft manufacturing and partly offset by a net $7.9 million downward cumulative catch-up adjustment on one contract [1]. Launch Services rose $73.7 million (59%) to $199.0 million on 21 missions versus 16, with revenue per launch of $8.5 million versus $7.8 million, and some revenue was recognized over time on Electron missions [1]. Implied segment gross profit, calculated as revenue less cost of revenues because segment profit is not disclosed, rose from $81.5 million to $126.0 million in Space Systems and from $34.6 million to $81.2 million in Launch Services [1]. Launch Services therefore contributed a larger share of the gross profit gain relative to its revenue base.

Cost of revenues grew 23%, lifting gross margin to 34.4% from 26.6% [1]. Cost per launch fell to $4.8 million from $5.7 million, which management attributes to scale efficiencies [1]. Research and development rose 55% to $270.7 million, mainly for Neutron, and the operating loss widened to $228.8 million, though operating margin improved to -38.1% from -43.6% [1]. The net loss widened to $198.2 million from $190.2 million, but net margin improved to -33.1% from -43.7%, aided by a $27.7 million tax benefit. EPS was -$0.37 versus -$0.38 as diluted shares rose 7% [1]. The gap between a higher gross margin and a wider operating loss shows that current gross profit gains are being absorbed by development spending.

Cash flow shows the cost of this growth. Operating cash flow was -$165.5 million versus -$48.9 million, capital expenditures rose to $156.3 million from $67.1 million, and free cash flow was about -$321.8 million [1]. The shortfall was funded mainly by $1,119.5 million of at-the-market equity proceeds. Year-end cash was $828.7 million, plus $270.2 million of marketable securities [1]. The balance sheet strengthened on liquidity, with the current ratio rising to about 4.1x from 2.0x and debt-to-equity falling to about 0.15x from 1.22x, but the accumulated deficit widened to $1,011.9 million [1]. Goodwill and intangibles rose to $430.5 million following the GEOST acquisition [1].
risk_assessment:
Government dependence and customer concentration is the first key risk. Government contracts are fixed-price, so cost overruns fall on Rocket Lab's margins. Governments can also terminate contracts at any time, and remedies may fall short of full performance, and some customers have defaulted in the past [1]. With U.S. government-linked revenue at about 47% of 2025 revenue and the top five customers at about 49%, a funding delay or award slip has a material effect. The October 2025 government shutdown, which delayed awards and payments, illustrates this exposure [1].

Execution and launch reliability is the second risk. Electron has flown 75 successful missions, but three customer launches have failed, in July 2020, May 2021, and September 2023, each resulting in loss of payloads and a halt until the FAA authorized resumption [1]. The Neutron Stage 1 tank ruptured during a hydrostatic pressure qualification test on January 21, 2026, pushing first launch to Q4 2026 [1]. The company does not maintain back-up manufacturing facilities, and its disaster recovery plans are limited, and insurance does not cover its own losses to vehicles, launch complexes, or spacecraft [1]. Because the launch services business currently depends on Electron and development contracts carry penalties and liquidated damages for delay, schedule slips translate directly into lost revenue [1].

Continued losses and capital access form the third risk. The company expects operating expenses and capital expenditures to rise significantly and expects losses to continue for at least the next 12 months [1]. Operating cash flow was -$165.5 million in 2025, and the company relied on $1,119.5 million of at-the-market equity sales to fund growth [1]. The share price, which closed at $70.20 against a 52-week range of $14.71 to $99.58, shows how volatile the equity funding route can be [2]. Aggregate indebtedness was $157.4 million at year-end 2025, and convertible notes may require cash repurchase on a fundamental change [1]. Dilution is a continuing risk from equity issuance, convertible note settlement in shares, and acquisitions. The Direct Funding Agreement with the Department of Commerce also restricts share buybacks and dividends without prior approval [1].

Taken together, these risks reinforce one another. A Neutron delay could slow revenue from government and commercial customers while losses and debt service continue, and a funding gap could force equity issuance on unfavorable terms [1]. The loss-to-revenue ratio improved from 75% in 2023 to 33% in 2025, a positive signal, but absolute losses have not fallen materially [1]. The filing does not provide contract durations, so the protection that long-term backlog offers cannot be fully verified [1]. Management currently expects existing cash, cash equivalents, and operating cash flow to be sufficient for cash needs for the foreseeable future, though this view depends on the execution items above [1].
competitors_analysis:
Rocket Lab was compared with three US-listed peers, chosen for business model first and size second. Firefly Aerospace (FLY) is the closest on launch services and national security missions. Intuitive Machines (LUNR) is the closest in size and provides space infrastructure and delivery services. Redwire (RDW) is a space-hardware and government-contract peer [4]. Planet Labs and AST SpaceMobile were excluded because their models center on data and connectivity, and large primes such as Northrop Grumman were excluded because they are far larger and more diversified [4]. Their market capitalizations of roughly $3.7 billion, $1.9 billion, and $1.8 billion compare with Rocket Lab's approximately $42.8 billion [2][4].

On the reported figures, Rocket Lab has the largest revenue base in the group at $601.8 million, and it grew 38% in 2025 [1]. That was behind Firefly's 163% growth from a much smaller base, but ahead of Redwire's 10.3% and Intuitive Machines' decline of 9.2% [4]. Its gross margin of 34.4% led the group, compared with 19.2% at Firefly, 5.2% at Redwire, and 2.9% at Intuitive Machines [4]. Its EBITDA margin of -25.8% was the least negative, against -45.9% at Intuitive Machines, -53.4% at Redwire, and -181.9% at Firefly [4]. Rocket Lab's gross margin rose in every year from 9.0% in 2022, while Redwire's fell from 23.8% in 2023 to 5.2% in 2025 [4]. The peer data therefore supports the view that Rocket Lab's unit economics are improving while several peers' margins are eroding.

Valuation is where Rocket Lab stands apart. Its trailing EV/Sales multiple was about 67 in 2025, versus about 19 at Firefly, 8.5 at Intuitive Machines, and 4.4 at Redwire [4]. EV/EBITDA cannot be computed for any company in the group because EBITDA is negative across the board, so EV/Sales is the most useful relative yardstick here. Analyst consensus rates the stock Buy with a mean target of $93.15 [3], but the market is pricing profit that has not yet arrived. Free cash flow was -$321.8 million, the largest outflow in the dataset, and ROIC remained negative at -9.3% [1][4]. Rocket Lab is the strongest operator in the group on growth and margin trajectory, but its valuation depends on converting that growth into sustained profit, which the historical figures do not yet show.
